sentences.text: This bird was roughly the size of a modern chicken, featuring a long skull packed with about ten teeth in the upper jaw and twenty in the lower jaw.
Its skeleton included a well-developed U-shaped furcula, commonly known as a wishbone, which aided in its ability to walk and fly effectively.
The sternum was elongated rather than wide to provide space for the large flight muscles required for powered flight.
Its feet possessed long toes with elongated bones and relatively straight claws.
Some individuals retained long feathers on their lower limbs, creating an appearance of having four wings.
Fossils of this animal gained notoriety when they were used in the famous paleontological forgery known as Archaeoraptor.
The name Archaeovolans repatriatus was later determined to be a junior synonym of Yanornis.
The genus Yanornis was formally named by Zhou and Zhang in the year 2001.
The type species, Yanornis martini, was described based on several fossils discovered in the Jiufotang Formation near Chaoyang.
Scientists have recorded four distinct fossil occurrences of this species to date.
Fossil specimens containing fish remains within the stomach and crop suggest that this creature was primarily a fish-eater.
One individual preserved a large quantity of stones in the gizzard region, though their exact function remains unclear.
The fish-eating diet and associated physical adaptations show convergent evolution with the distantly related enantiornithine Longipteryx.
Taxonomically, Yanornis is classified within the class Reptilia.
It belongs to the family Yanornithidae.
The order Yanornithiformes was established to separate Yanornis and related birds from other early Ornithurae such as Gansus.
A study published in 2006 found that Yanornis, Yixianornis, and Songlingornis formed a monophyletic group.
Some research suggests that the species Aberratiodontus wui is either a poorly preserved specimen of Yanornis martini or a close relative.
Yanornis inhabited Liaoning province in China during the Early Cretaceous, with fossils found in the 120-million-year-old Jiufotang Formation and the 124-million-year-old Yixian Formation.
The animal lived during the Barremian to Aptian stages, between 125.77 and 113.2 million years ago.
It is debated whether Yanornis could switch its diet between fish and seeds, as later studies cast doubt on the hypothesis that the preserved stones were gastroliths used for grinding seeds.
